newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerians register for polls to end military rule.
newsitem.headline: Nigerians register for polls to end military rule.

text.p: Nigeria started registering voters on Monday in preparation for elections designed to end military rule but the opposition says ruler General Sani Abacha plans to use the vote to keep himself in power.

In an interview with a U.S. newspaper last week Abacha did not rule himself out as a candidate in the 1998 presidential poll, reinforcing views held by critcis that the transition to civilian rule in designed to maintain his hold on power.
"The real agenda unfolding vindicates our position," said a senior member of the opposition NADECO, which says the transition programme is a ruse to perpetuate army rule.
The electoral commission says it expects to register about 50 million voters over 10 days in Africa's most populous nation of about 100 million.

At St. Peter's registration centre on Ajele street in central Lagos, one of over 100,000 registration centres scattered in 8,870 electoral wards nationwide, more than 150 people had registered within two hours of the opening.
"I'm registering because I want to make sure there is a change of government next year," said Ade Eniola, a young man queuing up.
The head of the centre said the exercise had so far gone smoothly.
But in the capital Abuja in central Nigeria turn-out seemed low. "We don't know where to go and register," said Malam Dauda, a school teacher in Abuja.
Nigeria's last attempt at democracy ended in chaos when the previous military ruler annulled a presidential vote in 1993.
Millionaire businessman Moshood Abiola, the presumed winner of the annulled poll is in detention and so are many other opposition figures.
Abacha seized power in the aftermath of the annulment and despite the many problems he has encountered he has promised to hand over to an elected president on October 1, 1998.
Political observers said the registration of voters was crucial to the success of local council polls set for next month and the presidential election due in the third quarter of 1998.
They said the level of awareness of the exercise appeared low but noted that the five registered political parties had stepped up their public campaign to get voters to register.

"Only your voter's card can get you the leader of your choice," said Roland Oritsejafor, state chairman of the Delta state chapter of the Democratic Party of Nigeria, at one such campaign in the area.
